extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters (patent attorneys/agents), in-house IP managers and technical staff involved in patent programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent drafters on developing offensive and defensive patent strategies, conducting design-around analyses, organizing client patent programs (training, disclosure forms, review committees, incentives, docketing), and complying with professional ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive blocking patenting to mount attacks on competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may employ their patents directly against any and all infringers; patents can be used to force competitors to design around or to license, and licensing patents outside a company's field of use can be lucrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider licensing opportunities beyond the owner's field of use; weigh the low direct licensing cost against possible litigation and risk of invalidation (if invalidated the patent cannot be enforced against anyone). Start licensing campaigns with small-to-medium players to build momentum rather than targeting the largest player first. When developing an offensive strategy consider types of infringement (direct, contributory, inducement) and doctrines like equivalents; prosecution history statements can limit later doctrine-of-equivalents claims so responses to office actions must be carefully worded and concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent valuation (real property metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent valuation can be usefully understood by analogy to real property: prior art is like public lands or lands claimed by others; 'location, location, location' applies — claims that map onto valuable inventions are worth more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent's worth depends on where its claims sit relative to valuable inventions (location) and on the quality of the patent's construction (how well it was drafted). Legal remedies are analogous to remedies for encroachment in real estate. Full valuation discussion is out of scope but the metaphor helps frame strategic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive patenting to protect against infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents function as 'swords' rather than 'shields'—holding patents does not guarantee freedom to operate but can deter suits if competitors fear counter-suits; patents can be used defensively to block competitors or as bargaining chips in cross-licenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defensive strategy may include acquiring many patents surrounding core products to create counter-suit leverage. Consider industry norms, patent scope, technical and business strategy; cross-licensing often occurs among major players and may include field-of-use limits that preserve litigation risk outside those fields. There is little reason to acquire patents without a specific business purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling exploitation options (per-product matrix)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use economic modeling and a simple matrix listing products to decide on a per-product basis how to exploit related intellectual property (defensive, licensing, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate likelihoods of success and managerial buy-in for each option, then analyze highest-rated options further considering patent strengths/weaknesses and market values. Choose strategy that aligns with core business and creates market entry barriers where desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-around techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Designing around patents involves determining the scope of claim coverage by detailed review of the patent, its cited prior art, and its prosecution history to identify limiting admissions or claim constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply jurisdiction-specific claim construction rules; consider ordinary/plain meaning, specification context, prosecution history, and means-plus-function consequences. Prepare detailed opinions when needed. Close analysis can reveal admissions that limit claim scope; the drafter should assist with interpretation but be cautious about creating potentially limiting client communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining noninfringement or invalidity opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys may prepare noninfringement or invalidity opinions to advise companies and in some jurisdictions to defend against willful infringement claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinions vary in length/detail; neutral third-party opinions may provide willfulness defenses where recognized. Attorneys often avoid preparing opinions if they believe the client is actually infringing. Patent drafters can assist attorneys by providing technical expertise for opinion preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling and confidentiality of patent opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney opinions are typically protected by attorney–client privilege and should be retained in strict confidence; sharing can risk waiver unless appropriate agreements exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not share opinions broadly; produce them only to necessary company executives. Relying on an opinion may waive privilege for related opinions. If sharing among parties, use a common interest or joint defense agreement — prepare such agreements carefully (beyond manual scope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation considerations (including means-plus-function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction rules vary by jurisdiction; initial interpretation often gives plain/ordinary meaning but may be informed by the specification and prosecution history; means-plus-function language requires special consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When performing design-around or infringement analyses, determine precise meanings of claim terms per applicable judicial and patent-office rules. Consider how courts in the jurisdiction treat prosecution history, specification reliance, and functional claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention disclosure forms: use and drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention disclosure forms collect core information about potentially patentable inventions and can be tailored to specific clients or industries (including company branding or docket numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept and preserve disclosure forms regardless of condition on arrival because of time bars; use them to capture inventorship evidence and best mode information where required. Consider interviewing inventors to fill gaps. Tailor forms over time to add value for specific clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks associated with invention disclosure forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Information in disclosure forms can be used adversely in litigation (e.g., to argue claim construction, to show inequitable conduct by failing to disclose prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train staff on how to complete forms properly; ensure invention disclosures and related information disclosure procedures are professionally handled to mitigate litigation risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Docketing systems and critical-date management
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish docketing (diary) systems to track critical patent-related dates (office action responses, foreign filing deadlines, annuities, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent drafters should maintain docketing for their own purposes and help clients establish procedures to avoid missed deadlines; docketing is a core component of internal patent program infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting inventions to patent (return-on-investment focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select for patenting those inventions that will yield the highest return on investment through licensing or increased product sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult a wider cross-section of skills beyond inventors (e.g., marketing) to understand commercial impact. Consider ease of design-around and how broadly the invention can be meaningfully patented; if a technically brilliant invention maps to low commercial value, prefer a modest but commercially valuable invention unless patentability is otherwise limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training management and marketing personnel about patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer learning opportunities to senior management and marketing teams to raise awareness of patent benefits and dispel misunderstandings; if a group session is not possible, engage individually as opportunities arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers are often busy; use ad hoc meetings and larger presentations when feasible. Include marketing staff in patent discussions because their input helps determine what should be patented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training scientists/technologists on patentability and inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure engineers and scientists understand what may be patentable, who qualifies as a co-inventor, and how to prepare invention disclosures; identify and empower patent advocates within the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide support for completing disclosure forms or conduct inventor interviews. Be firm when investigating inventorship — supervision or sponsorship does not usually confer inventorship. Know jurisdictional differences regarding inventorship and rights to be named.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting up an in-house patent review committee
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a committee of key scientists, engineers, inventors, marketing staff, and management to periodically assess invention disclosures and make patenting recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent drafter may sit on the committee to advise but should not drive decisions. The committee should meet regularly to sustain a dynamic patent strategy that reflects marketplace changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor incentive and recognition programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Compensate and recognize inventors to encourage reporting and maintain morale; compensation schemes vary (payment on disclosure, filing, grant; royalty sharing; lab investment), and non-monetary recognition (plaques, dinners) is common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design programs consistent with employment and securities law — some jurisdictions require disclosure of inventor compensation policies and specific statutory inventor compensation (e.g., Germany). Universities commonly share licensing proceeds; tailor programs to client circumstances and advise on legal intersections (seek employment/securities counsel when necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional ethics (general obligation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drafters and patent attorneys must abide by professional ethics codes in their jurisdictions, which typically mirror general legal professional standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarize with relevant codes of ethics; when in doubt ask 'Does this seem proper or fair?' — if 'No', reconsider. Ethics codes are not exhaustive; unethical conduct may still be malpractice even if not explicitly listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics rule (i): Never knowingly file an invalid patent application
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent drafter should never knowingly file an invalid patent application (e.g., time-barred invention, nonenabling description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It can be ethical to file applications that may provoke legitimate challenges (e.g., novel legal questions), but the drafter should advise the client of likely challenges beforehand. Avoid filing where one knows the application is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics rule (ii): Keep the client informed of developments
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent drafter must keep their client informed of developments in their applications and patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notify clients when office actions are received and before response due dates; ask clients to review draft responses before filing with the patent office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics rule (iii): Keep abreast of procedural and rule changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent drafter must stay current with changes in rules and procedures applicable to their practice and notify clients when such changes could impact pending cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor national/regional patent rules and inform clients of relevant updates that could affect strategy or deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics rule (iv): Honesty in communications with patent office and clients
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent drafter must always be honest in communications with the patent office and with their clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not intentionally mischaracterize prior art or facts. Example (a) (intentionally mischaracterizing a prior art figure) is unethical; example (b) (framing an ambiguous reference in good-faith argument) is likely ethical. Avoid advocating patentability when personally doubtful without full client disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics rule (v): Perform agreed work (partial)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent drafter should always perform the work they have agreed to perform and ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text interrupted in source. The rule begins the duty to carry out agreed tasks — implied obligations include competence, timeliness, and meeting professional commitments; follow jurisdictional ethics for full scope.
